title: 'Crazy Jimmy' went defiantly into shootout with police: Gangster ignored friend, probe told
article: Shortly before he was brought down in a hail of police bullets, violent gangster Long Duy "Crazy Jimmy" Hoang ignored words of caution and pulled out a handgun, says a buddy who was in his car.
The move by Hoang, who had tried to outrace police in a high- speed vehicle chase through Edmonton streets, proved fatal, according to evidence at a fatality inquiry.
"I saw him pull a gun from under his coat," Hoa "Ken" Tran told Det. Dennis McGeady hours after the man he'd known for 10 years was brought down by up to 16 police bullets.
"I held his hand with the gun. I told him life was more important. I tell him to pull over, but he tried to outrun the police. I can't do anything about it."
The comments are contained in a three-page statement by Tran presented at a fatality inquiry into Hoang's death.

Assistant chief provincial court Judge Peter Caffaro initially denied media access to the statement until his inquiry report was finished. But he said Wednesday there had been a misunderstanding and made the information available.
To avoid delays, Tran didn't have to testify after he asked for a Vietnamese translator.
Tactical team members chased Hoang for 14 blocks at speeds of up to 100 km-h on Jan. 5, 2000, following a failed attempt to stop him so they could check out a gun complaint.
Around 8:30 p.m. he lost control and crashed his Honda Accord into a Jeep at 149th Street and 89th Avenue, where Tran surrendered.
But Hoang, who had been smoking crack cocaine, grabbed a .45- calibre Glock handgun. He fired at least once from the driver's seat toward an officer ordering him to put up his hands.
The officer and two colleagues immediately poured 30 rounds from automatic weapons into the car, riddling the windshield with holes and blowing out the back window.
The 28-year-old leader of the Crazy Jimmies died in hospital 36 hours later. Tran, who wasn't charged, insisted he couldn't remember what happened.
"Before the car stopped I jumped out and I (lay) down. Then the police stepped on me and told me to roll over."
For Cam Fraser, it was an engagement party he won't soon forget. He and his fiancee were at the home of friends celebrating their happy news when they heard the Accord smash into his Jeep.
The group watched from the living room while police levelled guns at the car. "As soon as that first shot was fired, I hit the floor," he testified.
"The women ran to the kitchen and my friend hit the floor, too ... Someone knocked on the door about 45 minutes later telling us to be patient.
"They just had to make sure the scene was secure."
Hoang, who left a sports bag containing a machine-gun in the basement of Tran's home on 155th Street, had been losing his grip on his drug and extortion gang because he was using too much cocaine.
Officers chasing Hoang were warned he'd been threatening to confront police so he could improve his status in the organization.
But Tran told detectives his onetime roommate was stupid. "I know he is a troublemaker. He's crazy. I'm scared of him."
Const. Cameron Forstey testified Hoang's unregistered Glock was used in two violent 1999 incidents.
In one, shots were fired in a downtown noodle house at a man who escaped by hiding in the bathroom.
Shots were also fired as one car chased another near 100th Street and 80th Avenue. No one was hurt in either shooting.
McGeady, a 26-year Edmonton police veteran, testified he couldn't find anything that the officers trying to arrest Hoang should have done differently.
"Members of the tactical unit were acting not only in self- defence, but in the most responsible way possible given the circumstances they were under," he said.
